    Session · 7:00 PM ET · weekdays

    The Evening Court

    After the close the day's leads are scored against the tape, the Pyramid re-forms, every seat files on base, off base and a lesson — with your evidence on file in front of them — the dossiers refresh and the model population trains, with its numbers in the court's own appendix.

    What the court is#

    The Evening Court is the day's accountability session. At 7:00 PM ET (editable under Settings) boardroom.retrospective.run_evening_review() takes the day's completed run, scores every lead against the closing tape, re-forms the Pyramid on the realized returns, and has every seat — the fifteen graders, the Skeptic and the Executive, seventeen entries — write a personal self-review: where they were on base, where they were off base, and the one durable lesson they take. The entries go to each member's journal, the journals regenerate the member dossiers, and then — last, on purpose — the model population runs its nightly generation. You can convene the court by hand with Run evening review on the Boardroom page or from the empty Evening view. A run already journaled is skipped unless forced; the button forces a fresh set of entries.

    The court is preceded by the 18:00 outcomes job: realized 1-day and 5-day returns are recorded for every lead whose trading-day window has closed (short leads sign-flipped), the Paper League is marked to market, and the outcome model retrains. The court records outcomes again itself — cheap and idempotent — before it scores.

    How the court runs#

    Scoring against the close#

    For each lead the court fetches the session's close and computes the day return from the briefing price, signed by direction — a short that fell earns a positive number, and the view's footnote says it: "positive means the call was right". Option leads carry their contract label, the morning's last premium and a refetch of the contract's last, open interest and volume; the persisted row also carries a flat contract_last (the evening refetch when it worked, else the morning's). A close that cannot be fetched leaves the return unavailable rather than zero. The scored rows plus the market-at-the-close context go to evening_reviews, one row per run, replaced on a re-run — that is what the Evening view and the PDF replay.

    The court scores its own session, not the tape in front of it (2026-09-09). Every quote is pinned to the session being judged. Until round 44 the close came from the last row of a daily history, which is correct at 6 PM and wrong at any other hour: a court sitting the next morning picked up the following day's forming bar and silently scored the wrong session end to end. On the 2026-09-09 book that turned two winners into losers on the record — ORLY read −0.51% against a true +0.24%, META −0.38% against +0.79% — and moved a contract from +189% to its true +49%. Now _fetch_close(ticker, session_date) takes the bar whose date matches and returns nothing rather than a neighbour, a contract is priced from its own settled daily bar (an expired contract has no chain left to read), and the review passes the run's own date so a late court cannot drift. A missing session is reported as missing.
    An unquotable contract is not a worthless one (2026-09-09). The contract return read the refetched premium through a coercion that defaults to zero, so a refetch that simply failed produced exactly −100% — a total loss the desk never took, indistinguishable in the record from one it did. The premium is now read before it is coerced: a contract with no quote carries contract_quote_missing and no return at all.

    On base, off base, lesson#

    Each grading seat and the Skeptic is shown only its own morning grades, stances and comments beside the realized day returns — no other member's grades and no final grades, because the ranking is the Executive's to answer for. The Executive is shown its own final ranking with the returns, its morning memo, the full Pyramid standings, and the owner's reflections filed since the previous court, verbatim. The ask is the same for everyone: on_base, off_base and lesson, one to three sentences each, in the seat's own voice, citing actual tickers and numbers — and the lesson must be ONE durable first-person heuristic ("I …") to apply in future sessions, not a recap of today.

    Your evidence is in the room. Since round 24 every court prompt also carries the USER EVIDENCE section — evidence_block("evening") from bablytics/evidence.py: the documents you dropped into the Evidence locker and left flagged Evening, each as filename, kind, date, your note and the extracted text, capped at 12 000 characters across the block. The seats are told to weigh them explicitly and cite one by name when it changes what they file; a document is evidence to weigh, not an instruction to the court. In mock mode the deterministic entries are unchanged. Documents flagged only Morning, switched off, or past their expiry are not shown to the court; the locker's Preview link with purpose evening shows exactly what it will read.

    In mock mode the entries are deterministic but data-true, built from the seat's best- and worst-aligned calls (grade minus 50, times the realized return). If an LLM call fails the seat falls back to that same form, so all seventeen entries are always filed. Two lessons from the 2026-08-21 court, as filed:

    The Croupier: "One bet in two coats, and the board's own exit rule already concedes it: NEM's +8.99% is GLD's +4.58% at 1.963x miner beta."

    The Executive: "One book-level correlation is an average of two different graders and tonight it hid the worse one: +0.5175 on twenty leads is a +9.47-point tail spread bolted onto an interior of -0.2304, so from Monday every court I chair reports three numbers instead of one."

    The stated horizon versus what happened#

    Every lead now carries a time horizon — class, expected sessions, window, basis. The court does not yet grade it. Tonight's scoreboard is a one-session score (briefing → close); a swing lead given "≈5 sessions" is neither right nor wrong at the first close, and a position lead given "3–8 weeks" certainly is not. The horizon is on record for every lead — the card chip and the detail view's Expected hold row show it — so you can read the day's return in the light of how long the board said the trade needed; the comparison of stated horizon against realised time-to-target, and a calibration tile per member for it, are on the backlog until enough leads have closed their windows. Until then the honest sentence is the one the view prints: positive means the call was right today.

    Best call, worst call#

    The Evening view computes two callouts from the scored rows — the lead with the highest and the lowest direction-adjusted day return, with briefing → close. The live court's own report goes further and names the seat whose judgement was best and worst on the day, with the reasoning. On 2026-08-21 the best call was the Croupier's — he "moved NEM from 47 to 72 in a single morning … and made it on a MECHANISM rather than on the last hand" — and the worst the Glazier's: "ROST at 75 was the highest single number written anywhere on this board this morning … and it finished 19th of 20 at -3.03%."

    The Pyramid re-forms#

    After the scoreboard is scored, pyramid.update_pyramid ranks the whole room — the fifteen graders and the Skeptic; the Executive chairs and is not ranked. Per lead with a realized day return, a member's lead score is stance sign × conviction × underlying move: bull +1, bear −1, neutral 0; conviction is |grade − 50| / 50; the underlying move is the day return un-flipped by lead direction. Strongly right earns, strongly wrong bleeds, timid or neutral earns almost nothing. The member's daily score is the mean over its scored leads, stored per (member, run) in pyramid_scores; the standing is an EWMA of daily scores with span 10 sessions, cut into tiers (rank 1 → tier 1; 2–3 → 2; 4–6 → 3; 7–10 → 4; 11 and below → 5). Rank 1 is "in charge of the world today": the next morning every prompt carries its rank one-liner, the Executive is told to weight the leader's grades noticeably more, and the dashboard's leader strip quotes the leader's latest lesson. The Boardroom page draws the standings as a CSS pyramid with a crown on tier 1.

    Standing is two column ranks, or none (2026-09-09). A seat's rank correlation is computed within a column and never across two, because the columns do not measure the same thing: on the 2026-09-09 book the share column's returns spanned 4.76 points and the option column's spanned 146.64, so a rank pooled over both handed the option column essentially all the variance — "an option score wearing a room rank," as the chair put it when striking the construction. The court packet publishes a share-column rank and an option-column rank, and no seat may cite a pooled one. A seat whose grades had no variance in a column is unscoreable there and is ranked nowhere in it: the Watchdog's flat sheet used to sort to last place, which was an artefact of where a sort puts nulls rather than a measured result. Undefined is not zero, and it is not last.
    The court reports rank correlation, and says which one (2026-09-09). The packet published Pearson correlation under the label "rank rho" while the week's registered commitments were written about Spearman — caught by two seats who recomputed it by hand and got different numbers from the printed ones. Both statistics now ship, each under its own name, with the rank statistic as the headline figure the commitments are scored on.

    Journals and dossiers#

    Each entry is one member_journal row — member, run, date, on base, off base, lesson. On the Boardroom page every member card carries a JOURNAL strip (latest lesson and entry count; click to expand recent entries); the member page shows the full journal timeline beside the track record; GET /api/journal returns the newest ten per member. The next morning each seat's five most recent lessons are injected into its grading prompt under "YOUR TRADING JOURNAL — lessons from your recent sessions (apply them)", and into its Pre-Open and Midday prompts too — that is the loop. After the entries are filed the court regenerates the dossiers: one markdown file per seat under data/members/<key>.md with the journal, the grading history with realized outcomes, the Pyramid standing and calibration (also served as /api/member/{key}/dossier and .md). See Learning loops for what is and is not learned.

    The owner's reflections#

    The Pyramid holds the court accountable; reflections hold you accountable. A lead you marked TAKEN owes a reflection once its 1-day outcome lands — the dashboard banner says "✍️ N trade reflection(s) due — the court reads them tonight" — and the form asks what happened (always) and what you would do differently (required when the realized return was negative). Reflections written since the previous court are handed to the Executive's prompt under "THE OWNER'S OWN TRADE REFLECTIONS", verbatim, with the ticker, direction, 1d return and a favorable / unfavorable flag, and the chair is told to weave them into the day's lesson-taking. See Positions & trades.

    The models and training appendix#

    Since round 22 the court also trains. After the journals are on the record and the dossiers refreshed, it calls pulse.evolve.generation() for its own session date — the nightly generation of the five-member actor-critic population the Pulse consults — and carries the record home on a generation block. The step is gated by the rl_evolve_enabled setting (default on), every failure is caught, and a court that did not train says "training did not run: reason" rather than omitting the section; the block is written to data/boardroom/<date>/generation.json and a line is appended to data/rl/self-court.jsonl. The journals are the critical path; nothing in the training half can cost the court its work. From 2026-08-21's block: "NO CHANGE — child m6 (64x37x64 tanh, bred from m2) scored -0.37152 vs m5's -0.36626 on the held-out split; the population is unchanged and every member was still trained and re-scored."

    court_appendix.performance_appendix(run_id) then builds four read-only blocks for the court document, every number copied from the same database readers the Archive uses — never re-averaged or re-rounded:

    run_history
    The last ten completed runs — date, leads, average 1d return, average 5d return, winners — the Archive's own table.
    last_seven_days
    The last seven trading sessions: the book's realized 1d average and winners on each, plus SPY and QQQ close and 1d from the court's recorded close (falling back to that morning's context, and saying which). Sessions with no run say so.
    five_day
    The 5-day column with the count of leads whose window has closed; an open window is named — "5d window still OPEN — 2 of 5 sessions elapsed … closes on …" — never blanked, because a return that does not exist yet must not read as zero. The trading calendar comes from the cached SPY dailies, dates only.
    models
    Generation number, each member's architecture, fitness before and after tonight's training, who was bred, who died, whether the child was admitted, and the deployed-checkpoint line; when evolution did not run, one sentence says why.

    Where it shows#

    The dashboard's MORNING BRIEFING | EVENING COURT toggle switches the view and the theme: evening renders night mode. The header names the mandate the scored briefing was generated under ("Mandate: Swing", read from the run; nothing for a run that predates the setting). The Evening view shows the close-of-day index strip and regime, the best / worst callouts, the Scoreboard (rank, ticker, direction, briefing → close, day %, contract last) and The Court Speaks — one card per member with its ON BASE / OFF BASE / LESSON entry, linking to the dossier. Before the first review it reads "The court has not yet convened" with the run button. The Evening view also carries the Evidence locker panel, because what you file there before 19:00 is what the court reads. The Archive replays any past court; the Boardroom page carries the run button and the Pyramid.

    The PDF#

    The in-app Download PDF on the Evening view returns bablytics-evening-court-<date>.pdf — ink and green print design: market at the close, the scoreboard, THE RULINGS — what the chair decided and the number each decision rests on, added in round 44 because until then a court's binding conclusions lived only in the archive JSON and never in the document the owner actually reads — and the court's per-member ON BASE / OFF BASE / LESSON sections, encrypted with the password you give (AES-256 with the cryptography package, RC4 otherwise). On live-board days the fuller court document built in the day folder (build_evening.py) adds the appendix: a MODELS AND TRAINING section (the generation line, a member table with fitness before and after, the deployed-checkpoint line) and PERFORMANCE — the run-history table, the seven-session strip, the five-day column with open windows named — then the note to the owner and tomorrow's watch.

    API#

    GET /api/review/latest
    {"review": {run_id, review_date, market_close, day_report} | null, "journal_for_run": {member: {on_base, off_base, lesson}}, "members": [...]}
    POST /api/review/trigger · GET /api/review/progress
    Start a forced court in a background thread; the progress payload also carries last_generation, the one-line verdict on the night's training.
    GET /api/journal · GET /api/pyramid
    Journals newest-first (≤10 per member); the standings with score date, tiers and leader.
    GET /api/member/{key}/dossier · /dossier.md
    The dossier as JSON, or the markdown file as a download.
    POST /api/reports/evening/{run_id}
    Body {"password": "…"} → the encrypted court PDF.
    GET /api/evidence/preview?purpose=evening
    {"block", "chars"} — the USER EVIDENCE section the court prompts will carry tonight; the rest of the locker's API is on its page.
    Settings
    review_hour / review_minute (defaults 19:00 ET) via GET/POST /api/settings; rl_evolve_enabled (default "1") gates the night's generation.

    One date is one bet, however many legs sit on it#

    A ten-leg option column that all expires on the same Friday is not ten positions. The court that found this said so in one line — five legs on the front monthly returned −9.89% on a 74.79-point spread and five on the following week returned −1.628% on 39.49 — and it refused to read a gate that passed at exactly its old limit of five and five as a pass at all: a gate that passes at exactly its limit has recorded where the limit was set rather than constrained anything.

    So the rule tightened. A ten-leg option column must now carry at least three distinct expiries and no more than four legs on any one date. The pre-flight checks it before anything is written, the post-persist check re-checks what actually shipped, and the court packet logs every bucket — how many legs, what they returned on average, and the spread in points between the best and worst leg on that date — so the next argument about the number is an argument with returns rather than with a preference.

    When a date is full, the leg moves rather than the name being dropped. The column is assigned best-graded first, so the leg that has to move is the one the chair ranked lowest, not whichever name the pipeline happened to price first. The move is to the next date on that name's own chain — a stock whose front monthly is full usually has its own weeklies — and the moved leg prints its new contract by name in the pre-flight log. A leg with nowhere to go keeps its first choice and the book is refused: the gate reports what it did, it never silently drops a name the chair put in the column.
    The same court declined three tighter rules, and the reason is worth keeping. Seats offered a DTE ≤ 5 cap, a five-day rule and a revived premium floor. The chair refused all three: they are thresholds fitted on ten observations, and their own authors said so in the filings. This rule is about concentration, which is structural and survives a small sample; a threshold is fitted, and does not.
    It is a real constraint, not a formality. On the morning after it took effect, across forty candidates, exactly 29 names could carry a veto-clean contract on the front monthly, five on the following week, and one each on two later dates; nine could carry none at all. A compliant ten-leg column was just reachable and no more. That is why the chair's prompt now lists every date each name can reach instead of one contract per ticker — a chair that cannot see the dates cannot write a column that clears the gate.

    The court's rules become the builder#

    A court that writes a rule into prose has written it for the next chair to forget. Through the middle of September every ruling the court issued — the window stamp, the option-leg tests, the tie bands, the ledger — was carried as text in the next morning's prompt, and each one failed in the same way: it reached the room on the night it was written and not on the morning it bound. So the rules moved into scripts/boardroom/build_court_packet.py and gates.py, where they run whether or not anybody remembers them, and the packet the court reads is built by the same code every night.

    R14 — the window stamp
    The packet emits window_minutes, the minutes of tape between the freeze and the close, and every rho, mean and construction it publishes carries [W=<n>min]. A court on a window under a full 390-minute session publishes its seat ranks ADVISORY and writes none into a standing. The build refuses if the window is absent.
    R15 / R16a — what an option leg is
    A leg with no settled contract quote is UNQUOTABLE and dropped from its column — no column may substitute its underlying's return. For every priced leg the packet prints the contract's move against its underlying's with its sign, the excess in dollars, the intrinsic share of the premium at the freeze and the time-value drift. A premium change of a cent or less is FROZEN; a call that fell while its stock rose, or a put that rose with it, is WRONG-SIGN and struck; a deep leg (intrinsic at least 90% of premium) is tested on time-value drift of 2% or less, because a delta-one contract's move-ratio scatters around 1.00 on quote noise and a ceiling set at the true value strikes an honest print one night in two; every other leg keeps the 1.00 ceiling, labelled MARGINAL when the excess is five cents or less. The first version of this bound struck a 43-cent drift and kept a $1.59 one; the second reading fixed the test, not the number.
    R17i — two grades by token
    On a row that serves a contract block the grade field is the share grade and the comment carries G_OPTION=nn for the contract. The share column is scored on the grade, the option column on the token; a shipped option leg with no token scores that seat null on that leg, never its share grade. The builder prints tokens found over rows shipped, per seat.
    R19 — tie bands
    Seat ranks over a short window band greedily from the top: a seat joins the current band if its rho is within one standard error of the band leader's, else opens a new band. Ranks inside a band are unordered, and the packet prints the room's common read — the mean of the seat rhos — attributed to the room and to no member.
    R21 / R23 / R29 / R32 — one mark, one ledger
    The mark-to-market job runs once per court date. The session ledger lists every run id of the last fortnight with its status, its window and counts_for_clocks (judged, over a full window); a run that was built and deleted carries a tombstone — when, why, whether the open had passed and whether grades were filed — or is marked UNAUDITABLE until it does; a blank weekday carries a reason or is an exchange holiday by the served calendar; and a session no court ever sat on is a NULL JUDGEMENT, final, rather than a verdict written afterwards by a court that has read every close since. An option column with fewer than five priced legs prints its legs and no rho, no bands and no seat ranks.
    R22 / R27 — one median
    The share column ships on the room's raw median, and there is exactly one median vector: the gate that ships the book writes its members to disk and the court reads that file. A seat enters a median only after five judged full-window courts with a non-null rho in that column — before that it is SHADOW, printed beside and never inside — and a line whose comment carries ABSTAIN is null for that seat, never 50. The packet emits, per share line, the chair's grade minus that median and the session's sign, so a chair that runs above the room for five judged runs ships the median.
    R25 / R26 — sessions are counted
    sessions_to_expiry is served on every contract block: weekdays after the filing date through expiry, minus exchange holidays, plus the remaining tape as a fraction of 390 minutes. That count, never the calendar dte, sits under a square root beside a per-session sigma, and every reach-type token on any sheet prints sess=N or the provenance grep fails it. Reach is computed twice — the two-year sigma scaled once by the regime's turbulence ratio, and the 60-session sigma bare — and a grade moves on reach only when both put the need on the same side of 1.00. The desk's own formula, a per-session sigma under the root of calendar days, was the sixth desk figure the court falsified.
    R28 — the claims ledger
    A claim that settles on a date — a probability that a break-even is reached, a level a name closes above by a Friday — is written to claims_ledger.json when it is made and scored by the court that sits after the date, entering nothing before.
    R30 / R31 — one admitted set, and the benchmark wears the same stamp
    Every aggregate that touches an option leg reads the leg's status, and the build asserts that the expiry buckets, the headline and the column agree about how many legs were priced. Every published mean carries [n=]; the headline book is printed four ways over the same lines; a field holding a freeze-time quote is named _at_freeze. The packet serves SPY, QQQ and IWM at the freeze and at the close and their return over the same window, so no whole-day index change is printed beside a windowed book without it.
    R33 / R35 — the Pyramid and the chair's token
    A seat whose paper book has never held a position is UNRANKED and displaces nobody; the leader's read carries no extra weight; a move since a mark three days old is printed as since the last mark (3 days), never today. A chair share grade nine or more points from the median carries DEPART=±nn REASON= naming a served field no seat's grade already reflects, and the chair may not file above the median on a name more than 10% up on the day, with RSI above 75, or running against its own five-day move.
    The one that would have failed silently. The chair that wrote thirteen of these rules filed them under a key the carrier module had never seen (text where earlier chairs had written ruling). The module that exists to carry a court's rules into the next chair's prompt would have skipped every one of them and rendered nothing — the exact gap it was built to close, one key name away from opening again. It reads every spelling now. A rule that depends on a key name is a rule that depends on somebody remembering; the check that catches it is a script that prints how many rules it carried.

    Two returns, not one — the stock and the contract#

    The scoreboard prints two percentages against an option lead, and they routinely disagree by an order of magnitude:

    Stock
    The underlying's move, direction-adjusted — positive means the call was right. This is the forecasting number.
    Option
    The contract's own move from the premium it was opened at, and it is not direction-adjusted. This is the trade number.

    Why the second is not sign-flipped: a bearish lead expresses itself by buying a put, so the contract is already long the view. Flipping it would report a winning put as a loss.

    This used to be recorded wrong, and it mattered. Until round 30 the outcomes table held one number per lead — the underlying's move — for stock and option leads alike. Everything built on that table inherited it: the Pyramid, the model's training labels, and the Fund's performance. A lead that said buy the $610 call was recorded at the share price's +2.54% while the call itself went 1.50 → 0.95, −36.7%. The court was the only place that ever refetched a contract, and that price never reached the record — so the court's own transcript for 24 August calls that lead "the book's second-best leg at +2.54%", quoting the stock's move as the contract's result. Both numbers are now stored, and 100 historical rows were backfilled.

    What Monday's option book actually did, once both numbers exist:

    LeadStockContractEntry → later
    MRNA short $130P+2.67%−86.8%4.40 → 0.58
    DIS long $111C+2.05%+68.9%0.74 → 1.25
    WMT long $106C+2.21%−45.4%0.86 → 0.47
    MA long $610C+2.54%−36.7%1.50 → 0.95
    PLTR long $172.5C+0.19%−29.0%7.13 → 5.06

    A contract with no stored entry premium, or one that has expired and can no longer be quoted, shows a dash rather than a guess.

    The Pyramid still ranks on the underlying. That is defensible — it is a directional-forecasting score, and stance × conviction × the underlying's move is what it was built to measure — but after round 30 it is a choice rather than an accident, and the contract number now exists if the ranking should be based on what the trade did instead. Changing it would rewrite every standing, so it is the owner's call.
    See a real one. The courts, and the close-out books beside them, are published in the public archive — every session the board has run, readable without an account.

    The close-out book#

    A close-out book is assembled after the bell rather than before the open. Entries are the day's closing price, and the book it writes is for the next session. It is not a morning briefing and the document says so on its masthead — a fill tomorrow will differ, and no lead is graded as though it were an opening fill.

    It exists for the days when the next session is the one that matters. The 2026-08-25 book is the example: NVIDIA reported Wednesday 17:00, an hour after the close, with durable goods, the GDP second estimate and July PCE all landing Wednesday 08:30. Positioning in writing on Tuesday evening is the point.

    It files under its own name. A close-out book lands in runs/<date>/closeout-book.pdf alongside closeout-book.json, the close-packet.json it was built from and the slate.json the board graded. It is a run document in its own right, not a variant of the morning briefing.

    When the board audits the desk, not the leads#

    The 2026-08-25 book was built twice, and both sittings are in the archive, because the first one produced the most useful result this system has yet returned: the Skeptic scored his conviction at 14 out of 100 and refused to recommend anything — not because the leads were bad, but because he had found four defects in the chair's slate builder:

    • The rank field was alphabetical. The builder sorted the slate by ticker and then numbered it one to twenty, so the book's "#1 lead" was #1 for beginning with an A. Fourteen seats graded that document without noticing.
    • Direction contradicted the research. A call/put-ratio and RSI cutoff overrode the scan's own direction on six of twenty leads — while each lead's justification line quoted that same scan as its evidence.
    • Contract selection had no liquidity filter at all. It took the strike nearest spot ± 1 ATR and used the last trade if any existed. That produced a put with five contracts of volume all session on a 75% spread, a call holding 0.07% of its chain's open interest, a put struck exactly on max pain, one leg priced below its own bid and another above its own ask.
    • The ranking formula deleted divergence. It rewarded names that moved, so a name whose entire interest was that it had not moved could never rank.

    All four were fixed, the market closed, and the slate was rebuilt on closing prices. Option legs now must clear 500 open interest, 50 contracts of volume and a 15% spread, are priced at the ask — what a buyer actually pays — and are rejected outright when breakeven exceeds the chain's own implied move. 245 contracts were rejected for cause on the rebuild.

    The second sitting's Skeptic verified each fix against the code and the data rather than against the claim — re-deriving all twenty chair scores independently, checking direction on 20 of 20, and confirming every premium equalled the ask exactly — and his conviction rose from 14 to 34. It did not rise further, and his reasons are printed in full in the book.

    The audit is the product. A board that catches its own desk's slate-construction bugs is the system working, not failing. The first sitting's cross-examination is filed beside the second so the record shows why the book was rebuilt — and one of the second audit's own findings was checked by the chair and refuted, which is also in the document. Both directions of that are the point.
